content: Experienced laboratory technicians at our center were trained in HIV testing using Determine HIV 1/2 test kits (Abbott Laboratories) through a half-day training course. This training included instruction on the proper use of pipettes, the processing of whole blood samples, and the interpretation of test results. The trained counselors, who were midwives working in antenatal care (ANC) and delivery wards, had no prior experience in laboratory work. Laboratory technicians routinely performed the same HIV tests and provided the test results to the counselors. The reports generated by the counselors and laboratory technicians were compared, and any discordant results between the two groups were re-tested using the same rapid test kit and the same blood sample. Photographed rapid HIV test results were utilized in a modified external quality assessment scheme to evaluate the proficiency of result interpretation. This approach was also used to assess the feasibility of employing this method as the foundation for a quality assessment program for non-laboratory-based testing. A total of 148 participants, both experienced and inexperienced in performing and interpreting rapid HIV tests, were tasked with interpreting the photographed results of five different rapid HIV assays. The interpretations were scored based on the degree of technical discordance, and error scores were categorized according to each participant’s level of technical experience. In a study conducted in London in 2012, 39 laboratory personnel evaluated Determine HIV 1/2 antibody point-of-care tests (POCT) (Alere Limited, Stockport, UK). The study involved 17 false-positive and 17 true-positive serum samples, which were randomized into pairs, each containing one false-positive and one true-positive sample. Two independent readers identified each POCT result as either negative or positive and compared the line strength between the pairs. Additionally, six other readers graded the line strength on a scale of 0 to 5 using photographs of the POCT results. In a 2011 study in India, issues such as specimen mislabeling, contamination, and incorrect performance of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) were identified. All samples were tested using HIV rapid tests (Combaids), and only positive results were further tested using Tridot and EIA. The study reported a 50% discordance rate in results, with 8% false negatives and 86% incorrect results overall. In Cape Town, South Africa, in 2010, poor adherence to recommended testing protocols was noted. Researchers collaborated with local health administrators to investigate the causes of poor test performance and implemented corrective measures. The clinic changed the brand of rapid test kits being used and introduced quality improvement measures. Observations were made of clinic staff administering rapid HIV tests to real patients, and the estimated testing sensitivity was calculated based on the number of rapid HIV test-positive individuals detected by the clinic compared to those identified as positive by PCR or highly reactive third-generation ELISA tests. In Nigeria, the government’s first national HIV testing strategy was introduced in 2006. Five non-cold-chain-dependent HIV rapid test kits (RTKs) were recognized and combined in pairs to create eight different interim algorithms, which were adopted by stakeholders in early 2007. A survey conducted in late 2008 in Abuja, Nigeria, evaluated compliance with these algorithms and other laboratory quality essentials among HIV-testing laboratory personnel. The survey included 39 health facilities (15 public and 24 private) and used structured questionnaires to assess knowledge, skills, RTK supply sources, and compliance with the National Interim RTK Algorithms. Data analysis was performed using Epi-Info. In the Lake Victoria region of Tanzania in 2007, a survey of 89 health facilities (including hospitals, health centers, dispensaries, and voluntary counseling and testing centers) revealed that few facilities had standard operating procedures (SOPs) in place, and test kits were not readily available in some locations.
